tabs.title: Part Overview
tabs.text:
TECH UNIT 5 — PART 3 OF 3: INNOVATION — canonical legacy DayID family 30504
ONE UNIT, ONE GAME. Bring the SAME story-themed Falling Objects TurboWarp project from Parts 30502 and 30503. Give students ownership of an original mechanic/enemy/level change while teacher supplies safe tested advanced block patterns; finalize it for a family showcase. Technical independence beyond grade-7 Tech TEKS is not required to pass.
TEKS: Primary §126.18(c)(3)(B–C), (4)(B–C); supporting §126.18(c)(1)(E,F), (2)(A). No unsupported claim that block-only scripts meet §126.18(c)(2)(B) text-based program requirement.
Day1 STARTER 3050401: one mechanic idea, original feature card with story trigger, fairness and test; DAILY 305040130067.
Day2 PERFORM 3050402: adapt one teacher-tested code recipe (timed shield, increased fall speed, or extra enemy) and test; DAILY 305040230068.
Day3 PERFORM 3050403: playtest, debug, meaningful feedback and polish; DAILY 305040330069.
Day4 ASSESSMENT 3050404: short 4-section cumulative Major (305040439991–305040439994) then earlier Daily recovery.
Day5 FINAL SHOWCASE/RECOVERY 3050405: final playable saved Game Studio deliverable, short classroom arcade exhibit/family-share instructions under school rules, posted Major/Daily recovery; NO new ordinary mastery question.
Grade rules: one four-section equal-weight Major, regularly pinned DAILY, original receipt preservation and stronger-evidence recovery of same scores. Assessment must fit ~half of class. Finish one complete, stable player game, not an expanding coding wish list.
Student autonomy: original narrative, characters, colors, chosen mechanic and polish. Students may request a new mechanism; teacher can provide equivalent code recipe only after testing. Originality in design matters more than syntax mastery; assessment checks taught concepts and design reasoning.
QA: verify ALL individual HTML from approved master, correct Collector full keys/form, browser copy-before-Form, offline JISD byte parity and rendered accessibility; no student release without Captain. SOURCE OUTLINE ONLY, HTML NOT DONE.
Mode reconciliation — approved source repair 2026-11-12: Preserve the Captain-approved same-game daily tasks and dominant mode. Prototype Day 2's player controls are isolated teacher-guided new-tool practice within LEARN, not an additional independent project. On PERFORM days, place brief retrieval and the exact supported recipe in the work runway; do not add a second general Group Learn workload. Source teaching and tested code instructions remain available beside the required work. The approved Part-specific progression governs this build; no DayID, pinned question/rubric or milestone is changed.

tabs.title: Day 1
tabs.text:
DAY 1 | DAYID 3050401 | STARTER | Invent One Special Game Mechanic
LEARNING TARGET: I can turn one original gameplay idea into a rule and test plan because a designer's creative decision must work for the player.
Priority TEKS — In Our Words
§126.18(c)(3)(B): Plan, choose digital tools, build a prototype, and improve it through tests and revisions.
§126.18(c)(3)(C): Identify how people in different industries use a design process.
§126.18(c)(4)(B): Explain how worldwide trends influence the technology people develop.
§126.18(c)(4)(C): Use what you already know to learn an unfamiliar technology.
Supporting TEKS: §126.18(c)(1)(D): Work together on a flowchart showing a problem, solutions and a development timeline. §126.18(c)(1)(E): Compare debugging methods and apply one to improve an algorithm.
50-MINUTE RHYTHM: 4 min Warm-Up; 12 min Group Learn/demonstration; 7 min practice/prediction; 7 min academic DAILY; 15 min chosen project work/test; 5 min save/TEKS check/Studio. Shorten extras when real game build needs more time.
WARM-UP (participation full key 305040109998): What one surprise would make your existing falling-objects story game more fun without becoming impossible?
LEARN: The shared game already works; do NOT create another game. A MECHANIC is a repeatable rule that changes what players can do or how the world reacts. Examples: a shield with cooldown, a new faster enemy, or progressive speed as score rises. We will give everyone tested block recipes for these optional features; students do not need to invent new code syntax. A clear pitch states the IDEA, STORY REASON, TRIGGER, STATE CHANGE, visible FEEDBACK and TEST. Designers and developers collaborate: the student owns the creative goal; the scaffold/code makes it implementable. Industry trends include accessible difficulty, short-play mobile games, and hardware performance; do not assume every technical feature improves the audience experience.
GROUP PRACTICE: Teacher compares 'make it harder' with 'after every five safe dodges, the circle falls faster and the speed meter changes.' Students identify which is precise, feasible, measurable and linked to player experience.
DAILY ACADEMIC QUESTION — FULL KEY 305040130067: Choose ONE original mechanic or enemy for your existing story game. Explain its trigger, what changes for the player, and one fair test showing whether it works.
PINNED RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 accurate, original, testable and convincingly justified; 70–89 Clearly specifies a feasible feature, cause/trigger, visible effect and realistic fairness test; 50–69 partially developed or weak justification/test; below 50 insufficient. Missing work remains nonnumeric until evidence is assessed.
INDEPENDENCE: The student can answer using shared taught code/design examples even if their optional mechanic is not finished. One brief written response at most. Unanswered components still copy to the school Form as transparent gaps.
PERFORM (same ongoing story game): Create one-page Feature Card containing feature name, connection to story, sketch/screen location, before/after rule, triggered code recipe (shield, level speed or additional enemy), required art and two test cases. Copy the SAME game project before making modifications so its working milestone remains recoverable. Do not implement new code today.
CREATIVE STUDIO (one required separate Xtra zone; three taught-tool ideas): Draw an enemy silhouette; invent an upgrade icon; describe a dramatic level transition without coding it.
TEKS TEMPERATURE: independent confidence thumbs and optional detailed gap; separate Xtra.
MILESTONE: One implementable Feature Card that builds on existing game, not a new game.
SAVE & SUBMIT: Preserve existing TurboWarp project and original code; use only teacher-confirmed school artifact submission route. No unverified app/login links.

Teacher Reference / Evidence Alignment
Official source: Texas Education Agency, 19 TAC Chapter 126, Subchapter B, §126.18(c), August 2024 PDF, page 5. https://tea.texas.gov/laws-and-rules/sboe-rules-tac/sboe-tac-currently-effect/ch126b.pdf . Verified 2026-11-12. Evergreen target: TECH-U05-P03. Unit planning: Personal TEKS Roadmap, Unit Roadmap TECH Unit 5 row 6; dates remain teacher-only.

Explain its trigger, what changes for the player, and one fair test showing whether it works. The pinned rubric defines the limited reasoning evidence elicited here; an answer is not proof that the game ran.

tabs.title: Day 2
tabs.text:
DAY 2 | DAYID 3050402 | PERFORM | Turn Your Idea into Working Code
LEARNING TARGET: I can adapt a teacher-supported conditional, variable or event pattern because shared code recipes can help me realize a design idea.
Priority TEKS — In Our Words
§126.18(c)(3)(B): Plan, choose digital tools, build a prototype, and improve it through tests and revisions.
§126.18(c)(4)(C): Use what you already know to learn an unfamiliar technology.
Supporting TEKS: §126.18(c)(1)(E): Compare debugging methods and apply one to improve an algorithm. §126.18(c)(1)(F): Explain why repeating code or steps can make an algorithm useful. §126.18(c)(2)(A): Change and rename variables, and describe the kinds of data they store.
50-MINUTE RHYTHM: 4 min Warm-Up; 12 min Group Learn/demonstration; 7 min practice/prediction; 7 min academic DAILY; 15 min chosen project work/test; 5 min save/TEKS check/Studio. Shorten extras when real game build needs more time.
WARM-UP (participation full key 305040209998): A special shield should last forever after one button press. Is that a good rule? What could prevent abuse?
LEARN: In code, STATE stores whether a special condition is active; an EVENT or CONDITION changes state; visual feedback tells the player what happened. The class examines a worked shield recipe: make shieldActive and shieldReady for all sprites, set both to 0/1 respectively on green flag. On Player: when [s] key pressed, if shieldReady=1 then {set shieldReady=0; set shieldActive=1; say 'Shield ON' for 1 sec; wait 3 seconds; set shieldActive=0; wait 7 seconds; set shieldReady=1}. In FallingObject collision code, only deduct a life when shieldActive=0, and still mark hitThisFall to avoid repeat collision. Teacher-supported alternate recipe A: make gameSpeed start 5, increase by 1 at milestones of five SAFE dodges and cap at 10; use gameSpeed in downward y-change instead of fixed 5. Alternate recipe B: clone/duplicate a falling obstacle as an Enemy, independent randomized spawn and a different fair collision rule; do not count enemy misses as normal dodge points. Use ONE feature only; students choose the story-relevant recipe. Teacher verifies code recipe and demonstrations before guide build; this is specification, not automatically code QA.
GROUP PRACTICE: Teacher builds the simplest shield recipe, predicts state at 0, 2, 4 and 11 seconds, and shows the life-counter change. Students match event → state → feedback → test to their own chosen mechanic.
DAILY ACADEMIC QUESTION — FULL KEY 305040230068: A new shield is controlled by shieldActive, which changes from 0 to 1 when activated and later returns to 0. Explain what collision logic must check while the shield is active and why a timeout/cooldown makes the game fair.
PINNED RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 accurate, original, testable and convincingly justified; 70–89 Explains shield-state condition correctly and gives a sensible fairness reason for finite duration/cooldown; 50–69 partially developed or weak justification/test; below 50 insufficient. Missing work remains nonnumeric until evidence is assessed.
INDEPENDENCE: The student can answer using shared taught code/design examples even if their optional mechanic is not finished. One brief written response at most. Unanswered components still copy to the school Form as transparent gaps.
PERFORM (same ongoing story game): Choose ONE teacher-supported feature from Feature Card; copy exact verified code blocks into correct sprite, modify only named values/graphics tied to your story, test old gameplay first, then test new feature three times. Keep a quick before/after note for expected and observed result. If new feature breaks game, use same saved milestone backup and teacher scaffold; do not discard story art.
CREATIVE STUDIO (one required separate Xtra zone; three taught-tool ideas): Design shield visual feedback; choose level-up sound notation; sketch an enemy that fits the story.
TEKS TEMPERATURE: independent confidence thumbs and optional detailed gap; separate Xtra.
MILESTONE: One custom mechanic functions, while prototype movement, falling, scoring and lives remain intact.
SAVE & SUBMIT: Preserve existing TurboWarp project and original code; use only teacher-confirmed school artifact submission route. No unverified app/login links.

tabs.title: Day 3
tabs.text:
DAY 3 | DAYID 3050403 | PERFORM | Playtest, Debug and Polish
LEARNING TARGET: I can identify a game's real usability problem and revise it because meaningful testing turns an invention into a reliable experience.
Priority TEKS — In Our Words
§126.18(c)(3)(B): Plan, choose digital tools, build a prototype, and improve it through tests and revisions.
§126.18(c)(3)(C): Identify how people in different industries use a design process.
§126.18(c)(4)(C): Use what you already know to learn an unfamiliar technology.
Supporting TEKS: §126.18(c)(1)(E): Compare debugging methods and apply one to improve an algorithm.
50-MINUTE RHYTHM: 4 min Warm-Up; 12 min Group Learn/demonstration; 7 min practice/prediction; 7 min academic DAILY; 15 min chosen project work/test; 5 min save/TEKS check/Studio. Shorten extras when real game build needs more time.
WARM-UP (participation full key 305040309998): A player loses without understanding why. Is the rule broken, or is the feedback unclear? How could you tell?
LEARN: A meaningful playtest observes: what player TRIED, what they EXPECTED, what ACTUALLY happened, and what specific CHANGE is proposed. Compare a bug in CODE with a design problem in CONTROL, AUDIO, UI or DIFFICULTY. Test the original game loop and the unique mechanic separately before a full round. Use three cases: normal play, new feature triggered, edge/error behavior. Communicate rules with simple title and controls, visible HUD, readable game-over/restart feedback. Fairness does not mean always easy; challenge needs understandable rules and an opportunity to improve. A designer should prioritize one high-impact fix instead of adding ten unsupported features.
GROUP PRACTICE: Teacher runs an intentionally confusing shield demo with invisible effect; class lists two likely causes and suggests adding a visual indicator. Students state how an observer could confirm whether the indicator helps.
DAILY ACADEMIC QUESTION — FULL KEY 305040330069: Playtesters say a new difficulty or power-up activates without warning. Propose ONE change to make the mechanic understandable and explain a repeatable test that would show whether the change worked.
PINNED RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 accurate, original, testable and convincingly justified; 70–89 Identifies a specific feedback problem, proposes a relevant UI/rule correction and measurable retest; 50–69 partially developed or weak justification/test; below 50 insufficient. Missing work remains nonnumeric until evidence is assessed.
INDEPENDENCE: The student can answer using shared taught code/design examples even if their optional mechanic is not finished. One brief written response at most. Unanswered components still copy to the school Form as transparent gaps.
PERFORM (same ongoing story game): Exchange games for a structured 3-minute playtest, when possible. Record two observations and one priority improvement. Repair exactly one consequential problem, confirm the original rules still work, polish title, controls, sound (optional) and end/restart feedback without sacrificing completion. Save same project, capture change log before final review.
CREATIVE STUDIO (one required separate Xtra zone; three taught-tool ideas): Design a future update poster; sketch the player's facial expression at game-over; make a one-line trailer tagline.
TEKS TEMPERATURE: independent confidence thumbs and optional detailed gap; separate Xtra.
MILESTONE: A tested original story game with one distinctive mechanic, verified core behavior and clear playing instructions.
SAVE & SUBMIT: Preserve existing TurboWarp project and original code; use only teacher-confirmed school artifact submission route. No unverified app/login links.

tabs.title: Day 4 — Assessment
tabs.text:
DAY 4 | DAYID 3050404 | SHORT MAJOR ASSESSMENT + EARLIER DAILY RECOVERY
LEARNING TARGET: I can explain new mechanics, conditions, feedback and testing because reliable original game design needs deliberate decisions.
Priority TEKS — In Our Words
§126.18(c)(3)(B): Plan, choose digital tools, build a prototype, and improve it through tests and revisions.
§126.18(c)(3)(C): Identify how people in different industries use a design process.
§126.18(c)(4)(B): Explain how worldwide trends influence the technology people develop.
§126.18(c)(4)(C): Use what you already know to learn an unfamiliar technology.
Supporting TEKS: §126.18(c)(1)(E): Compare debugging methods and apply one to improve an algorithm. §126.18(c)(2)(A): Change and rename variables, and describe the kinds of data they store.
GRADE: ONE Skyward Major composed of four equal-weight independently submitted holistic sections, full keys 305040439991–305040439994. Allow ~25 minutes for short assessment and four school Form transfers, then previous DAILY recovery. Exact source/Collector question/rubric parity is mandatory. No extra registered mastery key or new project work during assessed sections.
STUDY & RECALL (nonanswer-giving, visible and usable throughout): mechanic, goal, trigger, variable/state, condition, cooldown, difficulty, testing, bug reproduction, usability, instruction, player feedback and purposeful revision. Use the concepts, not prefilled scenario answers.
SECTION 1 — Unique Mechanic and Story
FULL KEY 305040439991
STUDENT PROMPT: A game already has movement, falling objects and score. (A) Suggest one additional repeatable rule tied to its story. (B) Explain what player decision it creates.
HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 coherent creative rule, meaningful story connection and player agency; 70–89 feasible feature, sensible story relation and player effect; 50–69 incomplete cause/effect; below 50 insufficient.
Submission: original school Form with full key, complete assembled purple preview/copy first, capture partial/empty transparently; no submission blocked for missing academic answers.

SECTION 2 — Events, Conditions and State
FULL KEY 305040439992
STUDENT PROMPT: A shield uses shieldActive=0 or 1. (A) What should happen to a damaging collision when the shieldActive value is 1? (B) Give one fair way to end or limit the shield.
HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 correct conditional state reasoning, duration/cooldown and fairness explanation; 70–89 correct damage behavior and plausible limit; 50–69 partly correct; below 50 insufficient.
Submission: original school Form with full key, complete assembled purple preview/copy first, capture partial/empty transparently; no submission blocked for missing academic answers.

SECTION 3 — Debugging and Playtest Evidence
FULL KEY 305040439993
STUDENT PROMPT: A new enemy appears but a player reports losing two lives in one encounter. (A) Name a plausible cause or a useful check. (B) Describe a repeatable before/after test for the fix.
HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 accurately diagnoses repeated checks or overlapping scripts, proposes a robust fix/test and states expected observation; 70–89 plausible cause/check and repeatable test; 50–69 partial; below 50 insufficient.
Submission: original school Form with full key, complete assembled purple preview/copy first, capture partial/empty transparently; no submission blocked for missing academic answers.

SECTION 4 — Polished Game and Audience
FULL KEY 305040439994
STUDENT PROMPT: A family member starts your game without directions and quits. (A) Identify one missing information or feedback element. (B) Explain a design revision and how you would know the new player understands it.
HOLISTIC RUBRIC: Holistic 0–100: 90–100 justified user-centered revision with measurable acceptance test; 70–89 specific clarity fix and credible check; 50–69 generic or weak connection; below 50 insufficient.
Submission: original school Form with full key, complete assembled purple preview/copy first, capture partial/empty transparently; no submission blocked for missing academic answers.

AFTER TEST: Original previously graded DAILY correction and targeted reteaching only. New Major sections can be recovered after rubric feedback is posted for Day5 or a rescheduled opportunity.
TEKS TEMPERATURE: confidence thumbs across mechanic, rule, coding recipe, usability, testing; separate Xtra key 305040429999.
CREATIVE STUDIO: choose one short extension—sketch a sequel concept, invent a future enemy, or write a playful tagline—under one separate Xtra response key 305040420000; never part of Major.
HOLD: No assignment and no student release until all four reserved section IDs, exact prompts/rubrics, shared Form/Collector and visual/offline/CI QA verified.

tabs.title: Day 5 — Final Showcase & Recovery
tabs.text:
DAY 5 | DAYID 3050405 | FINAL GAME SHOWCASE + MAJOR/DAILY RECOVERY
LEARNING TARGET: I can finish and present an original working interactive game because design is a process of imagining, building, testing and sharing meaningful experiences.
Priority TEKS — In Our Words
§126.18(c)(3)(B): Plan, choose digital tools, build a prototype, and improve it through tests and revisions.
§126.18(c)(3)(C): Identify how people in different industries use a design process.
§126.18(c)(4)(C): Use what you already know to learn an unfamiliar technology.
Supporting TEKS: §126.18(c)(1)(E): Compare debugging methods and apply one to improve an algorithm. §126.18(c)(2)(A): Change and rename variables, and describe the kinds of data they store.
FIRST HALF (~25 min): Use SAME TurboWarp project. Final acceptance checklist: title and one-sentence game story; original protagonist/world/falling object; left/right control; functioning fall loop; fair hits/lives and one-score safe dodge; restart/reset; readable controls and HUD; ONE original featured mechanic/enemy/progression implemented with teacher-supported blocks; clear ending or replay loop; file saved and artifact submitted through verified teacher assignment. Students do short arcade showcase or reciprocal playtests (not a required separate new project), describe original story/feature, record one positive and one constructive user observation. If school account allows sharing/export, provide actual teacher-verified family demonstration route; NEVER promise public publishing or collect personal information.
SECOND HALF (~25 min): After Day4 Major result is POSTED with section feedback, select exact weak/missing assessment sections and answer them better in original Day4 guide/Form. Recover earlier DAILY original questions as appropriate. Stronger verified answers update same score. If teacher feedback is late, reschedule genuine Major recovery, use time for Daily recovery and productive game finishing rather than pretending it occurred.
EXTENSION FOR STUDENTS CURRENTLY UP TO DATE: create original game cover image, write a short design diary or draw a future boss idea, as authorized same-tool Studio Xtra. No extra assessed TEKS key; not conditional on buying/downloading anything.
FINAL PRODUCT: one polished, personally meaningful playable story game that students can show their families when the school's sharing method is verified. Portfolio reflection: 'My idea was __; my code recipe made __ possible; testing taught me __.' Reflection is separate from academic Major and does not replace submitted student evidence.
No changes to old student evidence or Captain's Show/Hide. No student release before Captain GO.
